artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus while electrons occupy shells; their charge and relative mass decide how atoms are counted and compared.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Before reasoning about atoms, separate each particle by charge, relative mass, symbol, and location.

steps.name: Place the particles
steps.beat: Show protons and neutrons clustered in the nucleus, with electrons animated on shells around it.

steps.name: Compare charges
steps.beat: Highlight proton +1, neutron 0, and electron -1 while a net-charge meter updates.

steps.name: Compare masses
steps.beat: Make protons and neutrons count as relative mass 1 while the electron mass is shown as negligible.

steps.name: Link symbols
steps.beat: Attach p, n, and e labels to the particle table so students connect diagram and notation.

key_symbols.meaning: Proton: +1 charge, relative mass 1, found in the nucleus.
Neutron: no charge, relative mass 1, found in the nucleus.
Electron: -1 charge, negligible relative mass, found in electron shells.
The central region containing protons and neutrons.
The region outside the nucleus where electrons are arranged.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Electrons fill shells in the O-Level pattern 2,8,8 for the first 20 elements, so a total electron count becomes a shell-by-shell electronic configuration.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Electronic configuration is a count of electrons arranged by shell capacity, not a count of protons or neutrons.

steps.name: Start with electrons
steps.beat: Choose a neutral atom or ion and show its total electron count before shell filling begins.

steps.name: Fill the first shell
steps.beat: Animate the first two electrons entering the first shell before any electron moves outward.

steps.name: Fill the second shell
steps.beat: Add up to eight electrons to the second shell and display the growing notation.

steps.name: Use the third shell
steps.beat: For O-Level examples up to calcium, continue with up to eight electrons in the third shell.

steps.name: Read the notation
steps.beat: Convert the filled shells into a comma-separated electronic configuration such as 2,8,8.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: In nuclide notation, the lower number is proton number and the upper number is nucleon number, so neutrons are found by subtraction.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Element identity follows proton number, while nucleon number counts protons plus neutrons.

steps.name: Read the lower number
steps.beat: Point to the proton number below the symbol and assign that many protons.

steps.name: Read the upper number
steps.beat: Point to the nucleon number above the symbol as protons plus neutrons.

steps.name: Subtract for neutrons
steps.beat: Subtract proton number from nucleon number to reveal neutron count.

steps.name: Use neutrality
steps.beat: If it is an atom with no charge, set electrons equal to protons.

steps.name: Name the element
steps.beat: Show that proton number, not nucleon number, fixes the element identity.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Chlorine has relative atomic mass 35.5 because chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 contribute to a weighted average using their percentage abundances.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of isotope masses, not the mass of one atom.

steps.name: Show the isotopes
steps.beat: Place chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 groups side by side with their isotope masses.

steps.name: Set abundances
steps.beat: Represent chlorine-35 as 75% and chlorine-37 as 25% of the sample.

steps.name: Weight each mass
steps.beat: Calculate 35 x 75% and 37 x 25% as separate contributions.

steps.name: Add contributions
steps.beat: Combine the contributions to show chlorine Ar = 35.5.

key_symbols.meaning: The more abundant chlorine isotope at 75%.
The heavier chlorine isotope at 25%.
Percentage abundances used to weight the average.
The relative atomic mass displayed for chlorine.
Mass multiplied by abundance, then added.

interactivity_hooks: Adjust abundance sliders that must sum to 100% and watch the average move.
Toggle simple average versus weighted average to expose the trap.
Click each isotope group to reveal its contribution to 35.5.

learning_design.core_aha: 35.5 is an average from many chlorine atoms, not a single atom with half a neutron.
learning_objectives: Students calculate relative atomic mass from isotope mass and percentage abundance.
Students distinguish weighted average from simple average and explain why relative atomic mass can be decimal.
Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of isotope masses, not the mass of one atom.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Relative atomic mass is always a whole number because nucleon number is whole.
target_misconceptions.correction: The isotopes are not equally abundant; chlorine-35 is 75% and chlorine-37 is 25%, so a weighted average gives 35.5.

target_misconceptions.misconception: The two isotope masses should be averaged equally regardless of abundance.
target_misconceptions.correction: The isotopes are not equally abundant; chlorine-35 is 75% and chlorine-37 is 25%, so a weighted average gives 35.5.

target_misconceptions.misconception: The more abundant isotope does not affect the average more strongly.
target_misconceptions.correction: The isotopes are not equally abundant; chlorine-35 is 75% and chlorine-37 is 25%, so a weighted average gives 35.5.

scenarios.title: Abundance pull
scenarios.guiding_question: What happens to Ar when chlorine-37 becomes more common?
scenarios.success_criterion: Student predicts the average increases as the heavier isotope becomes more abundant.

scenarios.title: Decimal trap
scenarios.guiding_question: Does 35.5 mean one chlorine atom has half a neutron?
scenarios.success_criterion: Student explains that 35.5 is an average across many isotope atoms.

scenarios.title: Free average
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you predict the average before the display reveals it?
scenarios.success_criterion: Student uses weighted average logic and rejects the simple-average trap when abundances differ.

checkpoints.prompt: A student calculates (35 + 37) / 2 = 36. Why is that not the chlorine value in the notes?

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: For neutral oganesson-294, proton number 118 gives protons and electrons, while 294 - 118 gives 176 neutrons.
artifacts.transferable_principle: For a neutral atom, read proton number for protons and electrons, then subtract from nucleon number for neutrons.

steps.name: Read proton number
steps.beat: Highlight the lower 118 in oganesson notation as the proton number.

steps.name: Use neutral atom rule
steps.beat: Because the question asks for an atom, set electrons equal to 118 protons.

steps.name: Read nucleon number
steps.beat: Highlight the upper 294 as protons plus neutrons.

steps.name: Subtract neutrons
steps.beat: Calculate 294 - 118 = 176 neutrons.

steps.name: Choose option C
steps.beat: Select the statement with 118 protons and 176 neutrons.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: A 2- ion with electronic structure 2,8,8 has 18 electrons after gaining two, so the neutral atom had 16 electrons and proton number 16.
artifacts.transferable_principle: To work backward from a negative ion, subtract gained electrons from the ion electron count to find the neutral atom proton number.

steps.name: Count ion electrons
steps.beat: Add 2 + 8 + 8 to show the ion has 18 electrons.

steps.name: Read 2- charge
steps.beat: Interpret 2- as the atom having gained two electrons.

steps.name: Reverse the gain
steps.beat: Subtract two gained electrons to get 16 electrons in the neutral atom.

steps.name: Use neutrality
steps.beat: Match 16 neutral electrons to proton number 16.

steps.name: Choose option B
steps.beat: Select the option with proton number 16.
